items.title: L6: Reading an advert for the details that change how you apply
items.source: Civil Service Jobs adverts; GOV.UK, Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Beyond the salary and closing date, an advert contains details that change how you should apply. The assessment section usually names the stages and says what is marked at each one. Often the sift marks only one or two behaviours, sometimes called the lead behaviours, while others are left for the interview. Many adverts give a word limit for each written answer, and you must keep within it. The advert may say whether you will write a personal statement, a CV, or both, and whether you will be asked for examples in the form of Situation, Task, Action and Result. It also states the contract type, such as permanent or fixed term, and whether the post is open to external candidates or to existing civil servants only. Look for the security clearance level and any nationality rules, because you cannot meet an essential requirement by promising to sort it out later. Adverts usually give the dates for sift and interview. If you cannot attend on those dates, contact the named person straight away rather than hoping the date will move. The advert also gives a contact for reasonable adjustments, and the earlier you use it, the more time the department has to arrange them. Read the whole advert before you write anything.

questions.prompt: An advert says only 'Delivering at Pace' will be marked at the sift, with two more behaviours tested at interview. How should Amy spend her time?

options.text: Write only the sifted behaviour and leave all preparation for the others until an interview invitation arrives
Give equal effort to all three behaviours, since the sift and the interview are weighted the same
Put her fullest example into the sifted behaviour, and still prepare examples for the interview behaviours
Prepare the two interview behaviours first, because interviews decide who is actually appointed

questions.hint: The sift decides who reaches interview, but interview behaviours still need preparing.

questions.prompt: Dev's draft answer is 340 words but the advert sets a limit of 250 words for each answer. What is the best action?

options.text: Edit it to within the limit, keeping the Result
Submit it and email the extra words to the contact separately
Cut the Result, since the Action and Situation are what markers score
Submit it in full, since markers read the first part and ignore the remainder

questions.hint: Over-length answers may be cut off or penalised, so edit rather than risk losing the best content.

questions.prompt: An advert is marked 'open to existing civil servants only'. Priya works for a local council. What does this mean for her?

options.text: She can apply if she explains her council role in the statement
She cannot apply, because council staff are not civil servants
She can apply, because public sector experience is treated as equivalent
She can apply for a lower grade than the one she holds at the council

questions.hint: Civil Service only means the person must currently be a civil servant.

questions.prompt: The interviews for a role are on the first two days of next month. Liam will be abroad then. What should he do first?

options.text: Not apply at all, as dates are fixed once an advert is published
Apply now and mention the clash only if he is shortlisted, since dates are rarely firm
Ask a colleague in the department to re-book the interview for him
Contact the named person before applying and ask about other dates

questions.hint: Raising a clash early gives the department the chance to help.

questions.prompt: Which clue in an advert best tells you that you should write STAR-style examples?

options.text: The salary section shows a London allowance for the post
The closing time is set at midnight on the last day
The location section names more than one office for the role
Behaviours are answered in writing within a word limit

questions.hint: Behaviour answers are evidence of what you did, which the STAR structure suits.

questions.prompt: An advert offers a fixed-term contract of 12 months. What is it most sensible for a candidate to check before applying?

options.text: Whether fixed-term staff are exempt from pre-employment checks
Whether fixed-term roles are assessed on a different set of behaviours
Whether it could be extended or made permanent
Whether fixed-term staff must repay the cost of their security clearance

questions.hint: Contract length affects risk and planning, so ask the contact about extension or permanency.

questions.prompt: Which statement about essential criteria on an advert is correct?

options.text: Essential criteria apply to external applicants but not to internal ones
A candidate who cannot show an essential criterion will normally be sifted out
Essential criteria are used only to separate candidates who tie on score
An essential criterion can be met after the start date if the candidate agrees to gain it

questions.hint: Essential means required, so missing one normally means no progress.

questions.prompt: Why is it risky to apply for a role needing a security clearance you know you cannot obtain?

options.text: Clearance is a condition of the job, so the offer would fail anyway
The department can usually waive clearance if the candidate interviews very well
Clearance is only checked for candidates who finish in the top few at interview
A refused clearance bars you from applying to any other role for a year

questions.hint: Clearance is a condition of the job and cannot be traded off against performance.

questions.prompt: The advert gives a sift date a week after the closing date. What does this tell Mia?

options.text: She can edit her application freely until the sift date
She can submit after the closing date as long as it is before the sift
Marking usually starts after closing, so early submission only adds safety
Early applicants are marked first and given priority in the ranking

questions.hint: Marking usually starts after closing, so the benefit of early submission is safety.

questions.prompt: Which detail in an advert should lead a candidate to contact the department before applying?

options.text: A note that several posts are available in different locations
A need for reasonable adjustments in the assessment stages
A salary range with both a minimum and a maximum shown
An instruction to hold a Civil Service Jobs account before applying

questions.hint: The adjustments contact is there so arrangements can be agreed in good time.

items.title: L6: Building STAR evidence from real experience
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; GOV.UK, Civil Service Behaviours
items.body: A strong behaviour answer uses one clear example and shows what you personally did. The STAR method helps: Situation and Task set the scene briefly, Action is the longest part, and Result says what changed because of what you did. Spend the most words on the Action, using 'I' rather than 'we', so the marker can see your own contribution. A good Result is specific, such as a deadline met, an error rate reduced, a customer helped, or feedback received, and can be small. It is better to use an honest example from a part-time job, volunteering, study or caring than to inflate a work example. Each behaviour needs its own example if you can manage it, because reusing the same story across several answers weakens the whole application, though a rich example can sometimes be reused with a different focus. Markers look at behaviours like Working Together, Communicating and Influencing, Making Effective Decisions and Managing a Quality Service. For Working Together, they want to see how you helped a team or colleague succeed. For Making Effective Decisions, they want to see how you weighed up information and chose, including what you did when information was missing. Avoid listing duties; describe one event and what you did in it. Keep the language plain and the answer within the word limit.

questions.prompt: Which part of a STAR answer should normally take up the most words?

options.text: Task, because it explains why the work mattered to the organisation
Result, because the outcome is what the markers compare
Situation, because the marker needs the full background to score fairly
Action, because it shows what you personally did

questions.hint: Markers score your behaviour, which is evidenced in the Action.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the strongest evidence of Working Together?

options.text: When two volunteers disagreed about the rota, I agreed a swap with each and the event ran on time
I have always been a team player and I enjoy working with all kinds of different people
My manager has told me many times that teamwork is vital in all of our work
Our team worked closely together and the whole project was a great success

questions.hint: It describes one event, a personal action and a clear outcome.

questions.prompt: Kate's answer says 'we reviewed the forms and we cut errors'. What is the main weakness?

options.text: It names a result, which is not allowed in an answer built on the STAR method
It hides what Kate did, because 'we' does not show her own contribution
It is written in the past tense, which markers tend to discourage in behaviour answers
It is too short to be marked at any level of the scoring scale

questions.hint: Markers score the individual, so the answer should say what 'I' did.

questions.prompt: A candidate has no paid work history. Which example is most appropriate for Managing a Quality Service?

options.text: Listing the kinds of job they hope to do in the future
Describing the club's overall aims and how it came to be founded
Checking a club's monthly accounts for errors, so mistakes fell
Saying they are a careful and reliable person in everything they do

questions.hint: An honest example with actions and a measurable result shows quality in practice.

questions.prompt: Sam has one good example about reorganising a stock cupboard. How far can he use it for more than one behaviour?

options.text: Possibly, with a different focus each time, though separate examples are stronger
Only if the wording is identical each time, to stay consistent
Never; markers automatically reject any example that is used more than once
Only if he adds a sentence saying that it is a repeat

questions.hint: Reusing a rich example with a new emphasis can work, but distinct examples show breadth.

questions.prompt: Which Result is the most useful for a marker?

options.text: 'It went well and everyone seemed pleased with the outcome in the end'
'I learned a lot from the experience and developed a great deal as a person'
'The task was completed in the end, though there were some difficulties'
'Orders were processed a day faster and my checklist was adopted by the team'

questions.hint: A specific, observable outcome tied to your action carries the most weight.

questions.prompt: For Making Effective Decisions, which element would a marker most hope to see?

options.text: How you weighed the information and chose, including when facts were missing
A long description of how your team and its reporting lines were structured
A confident statement that you have always got your decisions right
A full list of the policies that applied to the decision you made

questions.hint: The behaviour is about using evidence and judgement to choose between options.

questions.prompt: Why can an inflated example damage a candidate's application?

options.text: Examples should avoid mentioning results, because results cannot be verified
Longer examples always score lower than shorter ones, whatever they contain
It may be probed at interview, and dishonesty conflicts with the Civil Service Code
Markers prefer examples drawn from small organisations, which are easier to check

questions.hint: Interviewers can explore any example, and honesty is expected under the Code.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the weakest way to begin a behaviour example?

options.text: 'When the printer failed before an event, I had to act fast'
'My duties include answering emails, filing and attending meetings'
'During my volunteering, we received a complaint about a late delivery'
'Last March a missed deadline put a customer's claim at risk'

questions.hint: A list of duties does not describe a specific event or action.

questions.prompt: The advert asks for evidence 'from work', but Ben's best example is from voluntary work. What should he do?

options.text: Use it but remove all dates, so the marker cannot tell it was voluntary
Describe the role as part-time paid work, so it fits better
Leave it out, because only paid employment counts as evidence
Use it, describing the behaviour honestly as voluntary work

questions.hint: Evidence is judged on the behaviour shown, and misdescribing it would be dishonest.

items.title: L6: Understanding sift scores and what they mean
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; GOV.UK, Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: At the sift, markers score each answer against a published scale. Many departments use a numerical scale, with a higher number showing stronger evidence of the behaviour. A common arrangement is that a response is scored against what was written, not against what the candidate may be able to do, so anything left out cannot be credited. Candidates are then ranked. If the advert says a fixed number of candidates will go forward to interview, the pass mark is set by the number of applicants and their scores, so it can vary from one campaign to another. In a campaign with many applicants, a response that would have passed earlier may be below the line. This is why a rejection does not always mean the evidence was poor. Some departments use an initial check on essential criteria, followed by a scored sift. Others sift on the basis of a CV or statement of suitability. Markers are expected to work from guidance and to apply the same standard to everyone, and many applications are marked by more than one person or moderated for consistency. After the sift, candidates are told whether they are going forward. They can ask for feedback, which usually explains how the application compared with the scale. Treat feedback as information about this campaign, which you can use in the next.

questions.prompt: Why might a good application be rejected at the sift?

options.text: The pass mark can move with the number of strong applications
Markers are told to reject a set proportion of the applications they read first
Good answers are held back for the next campaign at the same grade
The pass mark is fixed for every advert at the same grade, so scores always settle it

questions.hint: In a competitive campaign the line moves with the number and quality of applications.

questions.prompt: A sift marker can see only what Zara wrote. What follows from this?

options.text: The marker will give her the benefit of the doubt on all behaviours
The marker will assume she did whatever the role needs
The marker will phone her to check the missing details
Evidence she leaves out cannot be credited, even if she did it

questions.hint: Scoring is based on the written evidence in front of the marker.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of moderation in a sift?

options.text: To hide scores from candidates permanently, even when feedback is requested
To raise every score in line with the best-marked answers, so all are treated alike
To help markers apply the same standard to every candidate
To let the hiring manager adjust marks for candidates they already know well

questions.hint: Moderation checks for consistency and supports fair marking.

questions.prompt: A department receives 400 applications and plans 12 interviews. How is the sift likely to be run?

options.text: Everyone who meets the essential criteria is invited, whatever the numbers
Applications are ranked on score and the line set to give about 12
Names are drawn at random from those who applied on time and met the criteria
Only the first 12 applications received are read, then the advert closes early

questions.hint: Where interview places are limited, scores decide who goes forward.

questions.prompt: Fiona was sifted out and asks for feedback. What is the best use of it?

options.text: Compare it with her answers and strengthen the lower-scoring behaviours next time
File it away, since feedback on one campaign never applies to another
Reuse the same answers in the next campaign, to show they were sound
Challenge the marker on every point mentioned, until the scores are changed

questions.hint: Feedback is useful for improving the evidence you give next time.

questions.prompt: Which feature of a scoring scale matters most when you plan your answer?

options.text: The number of people who applied in previous years for similar roles
The order in which the behaviours were listed in the advert
The description of what each score looks like
The grade of the most senior person involved in the marking

questions.hint: Scale descriptors show what evidence earns a higher score.

questions.prompt: A department sifts on a statement of suitability rather than on behaviours. What should a candidate do?

options.text: Write at length about why the Civil Service is a good employer to join
Leave the criteria alone and focus instead on their career ambitions
Reuse their CV text in the statement, word for word, to keep the story consistent
Show how their experience meets each criterion, with specific examples

questions.hint: The statement is marked on how well it shows you meet the criteria.

questions.prompt: Which belief about the sift is mistaken?

options.text: That feedback may explain how an answer compared with the scale
That a low score means the candidate cannot do the job
That the pass mark can change from one campaign to the next
That scores are based on the written evidence given

questions.hint: A score reflects evidence in one application against one campaign's field.

questions.prompt: An applicant meets all the essential criteria but is told they will not go forward. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Meeting the criteria guarantees an interview, so the department made an error
Their Civil Service Jobs profile was out of date
Applying early counts against a candidate in the ranking
Others scored higher and the number of interview places was limited

questions.hint: Meeting the criteria is the minimum; scores decide who is invited when places are limited.

questions.prompt: Why is a spelling and grammar check worth doing before submitting?

options.text: Markers must deduct a fixed number of points for each mistake they find
Spelling and grammar are the only things scored at the sift stage
Errors can make evidence unclear and suggest a lack of care
The system automatically rejects any application that contains an error

questions.hint: Clear writing helps the marker follow your evidence.

items.title: L6: Planning for tests and the interview
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; GOV.UK, Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Between the sift and the final decision, many Civil Service campaigns use online tests, an interview, or both. Tests may be verbal, numerical, or situational judgement tests, which present a workplace scenario and ask you to rank or choose responses. Practice tests are published for free and are worth doing, because they help you manage time, not just content. Do a test in a quiet place with a stable connection, and read the instructions before starting. If you need extra time or a different format, ask for reasonable adjustments before the test date, not afterwards. Interviews are usually structured, which means each candidate is asked the same questions and scored against the same criteria. Panel members score behaviours and, in some campaigns, strengths. Strengths questions are usually quicker and ask what you enjoy or find natural, for example 'What kind of tasks give you energy?'. Behaviour questions ask for a past example. Prepare by identifying two or three versatile examples and rehearsing them out loud, using STAR. Research the department so you can say why you want the role. Prepare questions for the end, and be ready for a question that does not match your prepared example, by taking a moment to think and choosing the closest one. Plan the logistics: the time, the link, identification, and travel for a face-to-face interview.

questions.prompt: Why is practising online tests useful even for a candidate who is strong in the subject?

options.text: It builds familiarity with the format and time pressure
It removes the need to read the instructions first
It raises the candidate's score automatically on the day
It means the same questions will appear in the real test

questions.hint: Practice builds timing and familiarity; questions in the real test are different.

questions.prompt: When should Hannah ask for an adjustment for a timed test?

options.text: After the test, if she scores poorly
As soon as she knows about the test, well before the date
On the day, if she finds she is running short of time
At the interview stage, when the panel can see the effect

questions.hint: Adjustments are arranged beforehand, not after the event.

questions.prompt: What is the key feature of a structured interview?

options.text: The chair alone decides the final scores after the rest of the panel leaves
Candidates choose which of the questions they want to answer
Every candidate gets the same questions and the same scoring criteria
The panel chooses new questions to suit each candidate's CV and answers

questions.hint: Structure supports consistent, fair comparisons.

questions.prompt: Which question is most likely to be a strengths question?

options.text: 'What kind of work leaves you feeling energised?'
'Give an example of a decision you made with limited information.'
'Tell us about a time you resolved a disagreement.'
'Describe how you handled a deadline that changed.'

questions.hint: Strengths questions are quick and ask about natural preferences.

questions.prompt: A candidate is asked a behaviour question and the prepared example does not quite fit. What is the best approach?

options.text: Answer a different question that happens to suit the example better
Pause, choose the closest example, and adapt the emphasis
Read out the prepared answer exactly as rehearsed, in case the panel notices a difference
Say there is no relevant example and ask the panel for the next question

questions.hint: A short pause and a well-chosen example is better than a mismatched script.

questions.prompt: How many examples is it sensible to prepare for an interview on four behaviours?

options.text: One separate example prepared for every question you can imagine being asked
Only examples drawn from the past month, so that they are fresh
None, so that the answers sound natural and unrehearsed on the day
A small bank of two or three adaptable examples

questions.hint: A few flexible examples are easier to remember and adapt than many scripts.

questions.prompt: What does a situational judgement test usually ask you to do?

options.text: Choose or rank responses to realistic workplace scenarios
Write a long essay on a current policy topic and defend it
Recite sections of the Civil Service Code from memory under time pressure
Describe your career history in detail, starting with your first job

questions.hint: These tests assess how you would handle workplace situations.

questions.prompt: Which is a good check shortly before a video interview?

options.text: Rewrite each answer in a more formal style, so it sounds professional
Test the link, camera and audio, and have ID ready
Wait for the invitation email to arrive on the day before checking anything
Ask the panel to send the questions in advance, to be properly prepared

questions.hint: Technical readiness avoids avoidable problems.

questions.prompt: Why is researching the department useful before an interview?

options.text: It lets you challenge the panel about current policy and show your confidence
It replaces the need for behaviour examples, since you can talk about the department's work
The panel marks candidates on the number of facts they can recall about the department
It helps you explain why you want the role

questions.hint: Understanding the work helps you give specific reasons for applying.

questions.prompt: During an online test the connection drops. What should Tariq do?

options.text: Do nothing, and hope the score is still recorded at the point where it dropped
Wait until the results arrive before reporting it, in case the score is fine
Follow the instructions and tell the helpline or department promptly
Retake the test on another device without telling anyone, to save time

questions.hint: Reporting quickly gives the department a chance to arrange a fair resolution.

items.title: L6: Reasonable adjustments and Disability Confident in practice
items.source: Equality Act 2010; GOV.UK, Disability Confident scheme guidance
items.body: The Equality Act 2010 requires employers, including the Civil Service, to make reasonable adjustments where a disabled person would otherwise be at a substantial disadvantage compared with others. This applies to recruitment as well as to the job itself. Adjustments in recruitment can include extra time in tests, an accessible format, screen-reader compatibility, breaks, written questions in advance, or a different interview arrangement. Candidates should say what they need, and the department should respond promptly and keep the information confidential. Many candidates are unsure whether their condition counts as a disability. The Act defines disability as a physical or mental impairment with a substantial and long-term effect on normal day-to-day activities, and some conditions are covered from diagnosis. If in doubt, ask the named contact. The Civil Service takes part in the Disability Confident scheme. Under it, disabled candidates who meet the minimum criteria for the role are normally offered an interview, which is the interview offer. Candidates usually opt in when applying. Meeting the minimum criteria does not guarantee a job, since the candidate is then assessed against everyone else. Adjustments should not give an unfair advantage; they remove a barrier, so the candidate is assessed on the same standard. Adjustments can also continue after appointment, in the workplace.

questions.prompt: Which describes the purpose of a reasonable adjustment in recruitment?

options.text: To remove a barrier so the candidate is assessed on the same standard
To make sure the candidate is offered a job once they have applied
To lower the pass mark for the candidate, to make up for their disadvantage
To exempt the candidate from stages they find difficult

questions.hint: Adjustments level the playing field; they do not change the standard.

questions.prompt: Nadia has dyslexia and needs extra reading time in a test. When should she ask?

options.text: On the day of the test, if she finds she is running short of time
As soon as she knows about the test
At the interview stage, when the panel can see the effect directly
After the test, if she scores poorly and wants it to be reconsidered

questions.hint: Early requests allow time to arrange the adjustment.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the Disability Confident interview offer is correct?

options.text: Any disabled candidate who applies is appointed to the post
The offer applies only to internal candidates already in the Civil Service
A disabled candidate who meets the minimum criteria is normally offered an interview
The offer replaces the sift for every candidate who opts in, so scoring is skipped

questions.hint: The offer secures an interview but not the job.

questions.prompt: Which is a typical adjustment at the recruitment stage?

options.text: Being given the role without competition against other candidates
Having the panel score the candidate more generously at each question
Skipping the interview and using the application on its own
Receiving the interview questions in writing shortly beforehand

questions.hint: Adjustments change the way an assessment is done, not the standard.

questions.prompt: Callum is unsure whether his condition counts as a disability. What is the best step?

options.text: Wait until the interview and raise it with the panel on the day
Ask a friend to apply for the role instead, who has no such condition
Assume it does not count and say nothing, to avoid any fuss at all
Contact the person named in the advert

questions.hint: The department can advise on adjustments and how the scheme works.

questions.prompt: How should a department treat information about a candidate's disability?

options.text: As information to share with every member of the team
As a reason to put the application on hold
As confidential, shared only with those who need it to arrange adjustments
As information to add to the candidate's profile for all employers to see

questions.hint: Disability information is personal data and is handled confidentially.

questions.prompt: Which is a correct reading of the definition of disability in the Equality Act?

options.text: Any illness that has lasted for more than a week, whatever its effect
An impairment with a substantial, long-term effect on day-to-day activities
Only conditions that stop someone from working at all
Only conditions that are visible to other people

questions.hint: The test is about the effect on day-to-day activities, not visibility.

questions.prompt: A candidate gets an interview through Disability Confident but is unsuccessful. What does this show?

options.text: The offer gave a chance to interview, but the decision was on merit
The interview must be repeated until the candidate is successful
The scheme was withdrawn for that candidate after the first stage
The department breached the scheme and the candidate should be re-interviewed

questions.hint: The scheme guarantees an interview, not an appointment.

questions.prompt: An adjustment was agreed for a test, but on the day the arrangements are not in place. What should the candidate do?

options.text: Tell the contact at once, ideally before starting
Complete the test and quietly accept a lower mark, to avoid causing trouble
Withdraw from all Civil Service applications, since the process cannot be trusted
Take the test without comment and mention it afterwards, once the result is known

questions.hint: Raising it at once gives the department the chance to fix it.

questions.prompt: What is true of adjustments after a person joins the Civil Service?

options.text: They are given only to staff on the lowest grades, where posts are routine
They can continue at work, such as changed equipment agreed with the manager
They apply only during the probation period, after which the person is expected to cope
They end automatically once the person is appointed, as the duty then stops

questions.hint: The duty also applies to employees.

items.title: L6: Gaps, references and pre-employment checks
items.source: Cabinet Office, Baseline Personnel Security Standard guidance; GOV.UK
items.body: After a conditional offer, the department carries out pre-employment checks. Most roles require the Baseline Personnel Security Standard, which checks identity, right to work and nationality status, employment history over the previous three years, and unspent criminal convictions. Some roles need more detailed security clearance. The aim is to confirm that you are who you say you are and that the information in your application is accurate. You should give accurate dates, the names of employers and reasons for leaving. If you have been out of work, studying, travelling, caring, or self-employed, say so; a gap is not a barrier if it is explained. Referees are often needed, and the department may ask for references covering the same period. If you have no recent employer, a teacher, volunteer manager or other responsible person who knows you may be accepted, but check with the department. If you have an unspent conviction, declare it as the process requires; many convictions do not automatically bar someone, and the decision is made case by case. Failure to disclose, or giving false information, may lead to the offer being withdrawn or, later, to dismissal. Checks take time, so respond to requests quickly and keep copies of documents ready.

questions.prompt: What does the Baseline Personnel Security Standard usually check?

options.text: Financial assets, political views and family history, going back ten years
Only references from the current line manager, with no other checks
Identity, right to work, three years of work history and unspent convictions
Only academic qualifications and professional memberships held

questions.hint: BPSS is a set of identity and history checks, not a wealth or opinion check.

questions.prompt: Jordan spent a year caring for a relative and has no employer for that period. What should he do?

options.text: Leave the year blank so that the form looks shorter and tidier
Describe it as travelling because it sounds more positive to a reader
Name a company he worked for, so there is no gap in the history
State it plainly as caring and name someone who could confirm it

questions.hint: Honest explanation is fine; inventing employment would breach the checks.

questions.prompt: Why do departments carry out pre-employment checks?

options.text: To decide which grade the candidate will be given on appointment
To confirm identity and that the application is accurate
To rank the candidate against others who are on the reserve list
To re-score the interview before the offer becomes final and binding

questions.hint: Checks verify the facts the offer relies on.

questions.prompt: Elena has an unspent conviction. What is the best way to handle the check?

options.text: Declare it only if the panel asks at interview, and not before then
Tell the panel but not the team that runs the checks, to keep it confidential
Leave it out, because any conviction automatically bars an applicant from the Civil Service
Declare it as the process asks; it is considered case by case

questions.hint: Honest declaration is required; many convictions do not bar someone.

questions.prompt: What is the usual effect of giving false information in an application?

options.text: The offer may be withdrawn, or later the person may be dismissed
The person is asked to attend a training course on honesty
Nothing happens if the person scored highly enough at interview
The department corrects the information quietly and the offer stands

questions.hint: False information undermines the basis of the offer and the Civil Service Code.

questions.prompt: Which referee is most likely to be accepted for a candidate with no recent employer?

options.text: A close friend who has never worked with them but has known them for years
A family member who lives at the same address and can vouch for them
A teacher, volunteer manager or other responsible person, if the department agrees
Nobody at all, since references are optional for every post

questions.hint: Departments often accept non-employer referees but confirm in advance.

questions.prompt: A candidate has held two jobs and one period of self-employment in the last three years. What should the application show?

options.text: Only the most recent job, because the others are now in the past
All three periods with dates
Only the longest of the jobs, since it is the most relevant to the role
Only paid employment, leaving out the self-employment that fell within the period

questions.hint: BPSS asks for a complete three-year history, including self-employment.

questions.prompt: Why might pre-employment checks take several weeks?

options.text: Departments only begin them after the start date, so they run on into employment
They are carried out only on the last working day of each month
They involve verifying documents and records held by other organisations
The department delays them deliberately to test the candidate's patience

questions.hint: Verification depends on third parties responding.

questions.prompt: How can a candidate help avoid delays in pre-employment checks?

options.text: Ask the department to begin without the documents and supply them later
Wait to be chased before replying, so as not to seem too eager
Send one document at a time as they are found, over several weeks
Respond quickly, send everything asked for and keep copies

questions.hint: Prompt, complete responses keep the process moving.

questions.prompt: A candidate leaves an employment gap unexplained. What is the likely result?

options.text: The department asks for more information and may delay or withdraw the offer
The panel is asked to re-interview the candidate on the missing detail
The vacancy is cancelled and re-advertised from scratch
The candidate is moved up the reserve list and the offer is held open

questions.hint: Missing history stops the checks being completed.

items.title: L6: Nationality, right to work and eligibility cases
items.source: Civil Service Nationality Rules, GOV.UK; Home Office right to work guidance
items.body: Eligibility to work for the Civil Service depends on nationality rules and on the right to work. For most posts, the Civil Service Nationality Rules allow UK nationals, Commonwealth citizens, citizens of the Republic of Ireland, and in some cases other nationals who have the right to work, depending on the role and on any transitional arrangements. Some posts, including many that involve national security, are reserved for UK nationals or have additional restrictions, and the advert says so. Do not assume that having lived in the UK for a long time makes you eligible; the rules look at nationality and immigration status. Right to work is a separate matter and is checked under the law on employing people. Candidates may have to show original documents such as a passport or biometric residence permit, or provide a share code if the person has a digital status. If a candidate's permission to stay is time-limited, the department checks it and the post may depend on it. Adverts that say a role is open to those with the right to work in the UK are not saying that sponsorship is available, so check the advert for any mention of visa sponsorship. If unsure, ask the contact in the advert before applying, rather than applying and finding out at the checks stage.

questions.prompt: An advert says a post is reserved for UK nationals. Maria is a Commonwealth citizen with the right to work. What does this mean?

options.text: She is eligible if her application scores highly enough at the sift
She is not eligible for that post, though others may be open
She is eligible once she has worked in the UK for five years or more
She is eligible, because Commonwealth citizens can do any Civil Service post

questions.hint: Reserved posts are limited to UK nationals regardless of the right to work.

questions.prompt: Which statement about right to work is correct?

options.text: It is a legal check that applies separately from nationality rules
It applies only to candidates who are not UK nationals
It replaces the nationality rules for most Civil Service posts
It is first checked at the end of probation, once the person is in post

questions.hint: Employers must check the right to work for all employees.

questions.prompt: Omar has lived in the UK for fifteen years but holds another country's citizenship. What is the best step?

options.text: Assume that long residence makes him eligible, as it counts for most posts
Apply and hope that the check does not look at nationality
Ask a referee to confirm his eligibility in a reference letter
Check the nationality rules and contact the named person

questions.hint: Eligibility depends on nationality and status, not on length of stay alone.

questions.prompt: A candidate's permission to stay expires in six months. What is the most likely effect?

options.text: The candidate pays for the additional checks themselves
The department ignores the expiry date until it has passed
The department checks what status they hold and how long it lasts
The candidate is given a permanent post automatically to avoid any gap

questions.hint: Departments check status and its duration.

questions.prompt: Which document is commonly used to prove right to work?

options.text: A utility bill with your current address on it, shown on its own
A reference letter from a friend or family member who knows you well
A printout of the job advert with your name written on it
An original passport or another approved document, or a share code

questions.hint: Specific approved documents or share codes are used for right-to-work checks.

questions.prompt: An advert says candidates must have the right to work in the UK. What does this not tell you?

options.text: That the check may happen after a conditional offer
That you must be able to work legally in the UK
Whether the department will sponsor a visa for you
That your documents will be checked

questions.hint: Right to work does not imply sponsorship, so check separately.

questions.prompt: Why should you check nationality rules before putting time into an application?

options.text: An ineligible candidate will be stopped at the checks stage, however well they scored
The rules vary from one interview stage to the next, so they must be rechecked
Nationality rules apply only to internal candidates, not to external ones
Nationality is scored as part of the sift, like the other criteria

questions.hint: Eligibility is a condition of the offer, not a scored part of the process.

questions.prompt: Which is a legitimate reason for restricting a post to UK nationals?

options.text: The hiring manager prefers someone who is from the local area
The role involves national security, and the advert says so
The role is based in a large city, where competition is fiercer
The department wants to receive fewer applications for the post

questions.hint: Reserved posts are tied to the nature of the work, not preference.

questions.prompt: Samira is sifted in, and the department then asks for her passport. What should she do?

options.text: Refuse until she is sure of her start date and the offer terms
Provide it as the department asks and keep a record of what she sent
Wait until the first day of work to bring it in person
Send a phone photograph in place of the original, without it being checked

questions.hint: Documents are needed to complete checks and the department tells you how to send them.

questions.prompt: Which statement about nationality rules and fairness is correct?

options.text: They are set out in advance and apply to everyone for the post
The interview panel decides how to apply them on the day
They can be applied differently to each candidate, depending on their record
They can be changed once the offer has been made, if the post changes

questions.hint: Consistent, published rules are part of fair recruitment.

items.title: L6: From conditional offer to start date
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; GOV.UK, Employment rights and notice periods
items.body: A conditional offer says that the department would like to employ you, subject to checks. Usually it states the grade, the location, the working pattern and a provisional start date. Read the terms carefully. A final offer is made only once checks are complete and you will receive a contract or statement of terms. Do not resign from your current job until you have an unconditional offer in writing, or you risk being left without a job if a check fails. When you do resign, your contract sets your notice period. Civil Service departments often accept that a new starter must serve their full notice, and a start date should be agreed on that basis. If your current employer will let you leave early, that is a choice for them, not a right. Salary on appointment is usually the minimum of the advertised range for new external starters, and departments may have flexibility in some cases. If you have more than one offer, be honest with each department about your timeline, and respond within any deadline they set. If you have questions about terms such as hours, hybrid working, leave, or pension, ask before accepting. Once you have accepted, keep in touch with the department before day one in case documents or equipment are needed.

questions.prompt: Why should Priya wait for an unconditional offer before resigning?

options.text: Her employer only has to be told on her first day in the new job
Resigning early cancels the pre-employment checks, which delays the offer
The offer can still fall through if a check fails
Her notice period only starts once she has begun the new job

questions.hint: Until the checks are complete, the offer is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Which items are normally stated in a conditional offer?

options.text: A list of the other candidates who were considered for the same role
A guarantee of promotion within the first year of employment
The interview scores of the other candidates considered for the post
The grade, location, working pattern and a provisional start date

questions.hint: Offers set out the main terms and the conditions.

questions.prompt: Tom has a three-month notice period and the department wants him to start in four weeks. What is the most sensible outcome?

options.text: He asks the department to pay his current employer to release him
Agree a later start date that allows for his notice
He leaves his current job without giving notice, to meet the department's date
He turns down the offer without discussing the start date at all

questions.hint: Contractual notice usually applies; the department can often be flexible on the start date.

questions.prompt: A candidate has two conditional offers from different departments. What is the best approach?

options.text: Tell each department that the other has withdrawn its offer, to gain time
Accept both and decide between them on the first day of work
Ignore the second offer until the first one falls through
Be honest about the timings and reply by the date given

questions.hint: Honesty and clear communication protect the candidate's reputation.

questions.prompt: Which statement about starting salary for external appointments is most accurate?

options.text: Usually at the minimum of the advertised range, with some flexibility
Open to negotiation without limit, if the candidate holds another offer
Set by the line manager personally, according to the candidate's wishes
Always at the top of the advertised range, for any successful candidate

questions.hint: Pay on appointment generally follows rules; flexibility depends on the department.

questions.prompt: What is the usual effect of a failed pre-employment check?

options.text: The offer is reissued at a lower grade automatically
The department pays the candidate while the check is repeated
The conditional offer may be withdrawn
The candidate is moved to a different role without discussion

questions.hint: The checks are a condition of the offer.

questions.prompt: Which question is sensible to ask before accepting an offer?

options.text: Who else applied for the role, and how did they compare with me?
Can I choose my own grade within the advertised range?
What are the hours, leave, pension and hybrid working arrangements?
What score did I get compared with others in the campaign?

questions.hint: Understanding the terms avoids surprises.

questions.prompt: After accepting an offer, what is a useful step before day one?

options.text: Confirm what documents, equipment and adjustments will be needed
Wait until the first day to ask, so as not to seem demanding
Ask for the interview scores to be reviewed before starting
Contact the other candidates to compare the offers they received

questions.hint: Preparation avoids avoidable delays on day one.

questions.prompt: What is a contract or statement of terms for?

options.text: To list the topics that will be covered in the induction programme
To set out the legal terms such as pay, hours and notice
To compare candidates who applied for the same role against each other
To record the candidate's place on the reserve list for the post

questions.hint: It is the formal record of the terms.

questions.prompt: A candidate is asked to start within a week but is not ready. What is the best response?

options.text: Accept the date and then not turn up, if it cannot be met
Ask the panel to re-score the interview so that the date can be changed
Withdraw from the process without giving the department any reason
Explain the constraints honestly and ask how flexible the department can be

questions.hint: Open discussion is likely to produce a workable date.

items.title: L6: Applying as an existing civil servant
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service HR, internal moves and promotions
items.body: Civil servants can apply for vacancies in other teams and departments, including roles at the same grade or at a higher one. Many internal vacancies are advertised on Civil Service Jobs, and some are open to current civil servants only. A move to a different post at the same grade is often called a level transfer or lateral move. A move to a higher grade is a promotion and normally involves a competition under the Recruitment Principles. Some roles are advertised as a loan or secondment, which is a temporary move, and the person normally returns to their original post at the end. Applicants usually need to tell their line manager, since release dates and references can matter, but the rules on whether permission is needed to apply vary by department. Applicants should not use official time or equipment inappropriately for an application, and must not use official information that other candidates would not have. Pay on a level transfer often stays the same, and on promotion typically rises at least to the minimum of the new grade, though the details differ between departments. An existing employee has the advantage of knowing the organisation, but must still be assessed against the advert and demonstrate each criterion with evidence.

questions.prompt: What is a level transfer?

options.text: A move to a lower grade at the same pay
A change of pay scale without a change of role
A move to a different post at the same grade
A promotion to the next grade

questions.hint: Level transfers keep the grade and change the role or location.

questions.prompt: Which move normally requires a competition under the Recruitment Principles?

options.text: A permanent promotion to a higher grade
A change in working pattern
A move between desks inside the same team
A temporary change of line manager

questions.hint: Promotion is subject to fair and open competition on merit.

questions.prompt: Aisha is a serving civil servant who sees an advert 'open to Civil Service only'. What does this mean for her application?

options.text: She needs no evidence, because the department already knows her work
She can apply, but she is still assessed on the criteria like everyone else
She is appointed automatically if she meets the minimum criteria
She can skip the sift stage, since internal candidates are fast-tracked

questions.hint: Internal candidates are still assessed on merit.

questions.prompt: What is a secondment in the Civil Service?

options.text: A form of voluntary redundancy offered to long-serving staff
A disciplinary measure used when conduct has fallen short
A permanent transfer to another department, with a new contract
A temporary move elsewhere, with the person expected to return

questions.hint: Secondments and loans are time-limited moves.

questions.prompt: Which action is inappropriate for an internal candidate?

options.text: Using confidential papers that other candidates cannot see
Telling their line manager that they have applied
Asking the contact named in the advert about the role
Using their own evidence to answer the behaviours

questions.hint: Using information not available to others undermines fair competition.

questions.prompt: Why might a candidate tell their line manager about an application?

options.text: The manager decides who is shortlisted in internal competitions
The manager can adjust the sift scores of their own team members
Release dates, references and planning may need the manager's input
The manager's permission is a legal requirement in all departments

questions.hint: Managers often need to know about timing and references, but rules vary.

questions.prompt: What does pay on promotion usually look like?

options.text: Pay stays exactly the same until the end of the probation period
Pay rises at least to the minimum of the new grade
Pay is halved until the person has completed six months in post
Pay is chosen by the candidate at the offer stage

questions.hint: Promotion generally means moving into the new pay range.

questions.prompt: Daniel is a serving civil servant. What does his experience in the organisation mean for the evidence he must give?

options.text: Having been in the same post for over a year is enough
His line manager supporting the application in writing is enough
Internal candidates skip the sift and go straight to interview
He must still show each criterion with evidence

questions.hint: Merit means assessment against the criteria for every candidate.

questions.prompt: Which of these is usually the case for a loan?

options.text: It ends the person's employment with the first department
It is temporary, and the person returns to their original post
It carries no arrangements for pay or terms during the move
It is permanent, and the original post is closed

questions.hint: A loan is a short-term move.

questions.prompt: An internal candidate wants to complete an application in work time. What is the best practice?

options.text: Use official email to ask people to support the application
Use work time freely, because it is a Civil Service job being applied for
Follow local rules and avoid using work time or equipment unless allowed
Ask colleagues to complete the form for them while they work

questions.hint: Use of official time is governed by local rules; the Code requires proper use of resources.

items.title: L6: Rejection, feedback and trying again
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; GOV.UK, Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Most candidates are rejected at some point. How you respond shapes your next application. First, read the outcome email carefully; it may say at which stage you were stopped, and it should explain how to ask for feedback. Feedback is usually available for candidates who reach the later stages and is often available after sift. Ask promptly, because departments may hold feedback only for a limited time. Use it to compare what you wrote with the scoring guidance. If feedback says that an answer lacked detail on your personal actions, change the way you write about the Action. If feedback says you gave a good answer but others scored higher, that may mean nothing more than a competitive campaign. Keep a log of applications, scores and feedback, because patterns appear over several attempts. Some departments allow you to be placed on a reserve list if you passed the interview but were not offered a post; a reserve list typically lasts for a set period, such as twelve months, and you may be offered a role if a vacancy arises. There is generally no penalty for reapplying to later campaigns, though check the advert for any limits. Treat each application as practice, and do not take a rejection as a verdict on your ability.

questions.prompt: What is the best first step after receiving a rejection email?

options.text: Delete the account and start again with a fresh profile
Reply at once to challenge the panel's decision
Apply for the same role again the next day
Read it for the stage reached and how to ask for feedback

questions.hint: The email often explains the stage and next steps.

questions.prompt: Feedback says 'the examples lacked detail on your own actions'. What should Ola change?

options.text: Write more about what she personally did, using 'I'
Make all her answers shorter and tighter
Use 'we' more often to show teamwork
Remove the Result section from each answer

questions.hint: Feedback points to the part of the answer to strengthen.

questions.prompt: What does being on a reserve list usually mean?

options.text: Has been moved to a different department, which will make its own offer
Will be offered a role within a week, once the current vacancies are filled
Was rejected at the interview, but the department keeps the application on file
Passed the assessment but no post was free; may be offered one within the list period

questions.hint: Reserve lists provide a pool of appointable candidates.

questions.prompt: How long does a reserve list commonly last?

options.text: Ten years, in line with the length of the record
A single week, until the next campaign opens
A set period such as twelve months
Until the candidate resigns from another job

questions.hint: Lists usually have a defined life.

questions.prompt: Why keep a log of applications, scores and feedback?

options.text: Patterns across several applications show what to improve
A log is required to enter the next campaign
It lets you compare yourself with other candidates by name
It helps the panel find your earlier results

questions.hint: A log lets you see what works and what does not.

questions.prompt: Which view of a rejection is the most useful?

options.text: It shows the panel was biased against you, and a complaint should follow
It shows how this application compared in this campaign, and informs the next
It proves you are unsuited to the Civil Service, and further attempts will fail
It means you should stop applying for a year, to let the record clear

questions.hint: Rejections reflect a specific campaign and evidence, not ability.

questions.prompt: Why request feedback promptly?

options.text: Departments may keep it only for a limited time
It is required before any further application is accepted
It is only available after thirty days have passed
Asking early changes the result, as the panel can reconsider

questions.hint: Time limits on feedback can apply.

questions.prompt: Feedback says 'a good answer but others scored higher'. What is the most reasonable conclusion?

options.text: The panel made a mistake and the score should have been higher
The answer was dishonest and should have been checked
The campaign was competitive and the pass mark was set by the field
The answer was over the word limit and was penalised

questions.hint: In competitive campaigns, good answers can still miss out.

questions.prompt: What penalty is there normally for reapplying to a later campaign?

options.text: Always, for twelve months after any rejection
Not usually, though the advert may state limits
Internal candidates only, after a rejection
Candidates who are rejected twice are blacklisted

questions.hint: Reapplying is normal; check the advert for any specific rule.

questions.prompt: Which approach to feedback is unhelpful?

options.text: Noting repeated comments across several attempts
Asking the contact to clarify any comments that are unclear
Comparing the feedback with the scoring guidance
Arguing over every score and changing nothing in the next application

questions.hint: Feedback only helps if used.

items.title: L6: Spotting unfairness and what to do about it
items.source: Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: The Recruitment Principles require that appointments are made on merit, on the basis of fair and open competition. Merit means the person best able to do the job at the level required. Fair means candidates are assessed in the same way against the same criteria. Open means the vacancy is advertised so that those who might be eligible can apply. The Civil Service Commission regulates compliance and publishes the Recruitment Principles. Examples of unfairness include a panel member scoring a close friend without declaring it, questions that are different for different candidates, criteria changing after the closing date, or a post being filled without being advertised when the Principles require it. Not every disappointment is unfairness: a decision you disagree with, if made properly, is not a breach. If you believe the process was unfair, raise it first with the department using its complaints procedure, setting out the facts clearly. If you are not satisfied after that, you may bring a complaint about a breach of the Recruitment Principles to the Civil Service Commission. The Commission looks at whether the Principles were followed, not at whether it would have scored the candidate differently. Keep copies of emails and notes, and describe what happened rather than guessing at motives.

questions.prompt: What does 'open' competition mean under the Recruitment Principles?

options.text: Only internal staff are told about the vacancy
The vacancy is advertised so that eligible people can apply
The interview is held in public, so that anyone can watch
Anyone can start work without being assessed on merit

questions.hint: Open means that those who might be eligible have the chance to apply.

questions.prompt: Which situation is a possible breach of the Recruitment Principles?

options.text: A candidate is told why they were unsuccessful, on request
Candidates are given the same amount of time at interview
A panel scores candidates against the same published criteria
A panel member scores a close friend and does not declare it

questions.hint: Undeclared conflicts of interest threaten fairness.

questions.prompt: A candidate disagrees with a score but the process was followed correctly. Is this normally a breach?

options.text: It is a breach if the candidate is already a civil servant
It is a breach if the panel had more than three members
A disagreement with a properly reached judgement is not a breach in itself
Any low score a candidate disagrees with is a breach of the Principles

questions.hint: Complaints must be about the process, not just the outcome.

questions.prompt: What should a candidate do first if they believe a process was unfair?

options.text: Raise it with the department using its complaints procedure
Write to the Civil Service Commission without telling the department
Go straight to the media
Withdraw from all Civil Service work

questions.hint: The department is normally given the chance to respond first.

questions.prompt: What does the Civil Service Commission consider in a recruitment complaint?

options.text: Whether it would have given the candidate a higher score
Whether the Recruitment Principles were followed
Whether the candidate is a good fit for the department
Whether the interview ran to time

questions.hint: The Commission checks compliance, not individual scores.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a fair recruitment practice?

options.text: Allowing some candidates extra preparation not offered to others
Filling the role without an advert when the Principles require one
Assessing every candidate against the same published criteria
Changing the criteria after seeing who applied

questions.hint: Consistency and transparency are core to fairness.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate describe a concern about unfairness in a complaint?

options.text: Contact every panel member privately, to ask for their reasons
Accuse the panel of bias, even where there is little evidence
Give opinions about the panel's character rather than events
Set out the facts clearly and avoid guessing at motives

questions.hint: Facts are easier to investigate than assumptions.

questions.prompt: Why should a candidate keep copies of emails and notes?

options.text: They can support a complaint with evidence
They are required to enter the next campaign
They replace the application form
They give the candidate a higher score

questions.hint: Evidence makes a complaint stronger.

questions.prompt: An advert changes the essential criteria after the closing date, disadvantaging some who applied. What is the main concern?

options.text: The delay it will cause to the planned start date
The cost of reprinting and republishing the advert
The length of the revised advert on the website
Fairness, since candidates applied on one basis and were assessed on another

questions.hint: Changing criteria late can disadvantage those who applied on the original basis.

questions.prompt: Which best describes merit?

options.text: Selecting the person who has been in the Civil Service longest
Selecting the person best able to do the job at the level required
Selecting the person nominated by the line manager
Selecting the person who applied first, in order of receipt

questions.hint: Merit relates to ability to do the job.

items.title: L6: Staying organised between application and outcome
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; GOV.UK, Civil Service recruitment
items.body: Once an application is submitted, the work is not over. Civil Service campaigns can take weeks or months between the closing date and the final outcome, and stages may be announced at short notice. Keep your Civil Service Jobs account details current, check your email, including any junk folder, and look at the account regularly, since invitations to tests and interviews are sent there and often carry a deadline for replying. Respond to every invitation promptly, even if only to confirm attendance. Keep a copy of what you submitted, because the interview often returns to your written examples and you will need to remember exactly what you claimed. Note the dates of each stage in a calendar and set reminders. If something changes in your circumstances, such as a move of address, a change of phone number or a new job offer, tell the recruitment contact. Do not contact panel members directly, and avoid chasing for results before the date given in the advert, but if the date has passed with no news a polite query to the named contact is reasonable. While waiting, continue to apply for other suitable roles and to practise. Be ready for the possibility that a stage is cancelled, rescheduled or merged with another, and read each message fully. Respect confidentiality: do not share test content or interview questions online, since doing so can breach the rules of the process and disadvantage other candidates.

questions.prompt: After submitting an application, which habit best protects Isla from missing an invitation to a test?

options.text: Checking her account and email, including the junk folder, regularly
Checking only the Civil Service Jobs home page for new adverts
Checking once a week on the day the advert said results were due
Waiting for a text message before looking at any email

questions.hint: Invitations arrive by the account and email, and often have a reply deadline.

questions.prompt: Why should Isla keep a copy of what she submitted?

options.text: It proves to the panel that she met the closing date
The department will ask her to resubmit it at the offer stage
The interview often returns to her written examples, so she needs to recall what she claimed
The copy can be sent in place of a CV when she applies elsewhere

questions.hint: Interviewers explore the examples you wrote, so consistency matters.

questions.prompt: An invitation to a test arrives with a three-day deadline to reply. What is the sensible response?

options.text: Reply on the final day, so that the choice is not rushed
Reply promptly to confirm, and note the date in her calendar
Reply only if she feels fully prepared for the test
Wait for a reminder email before responding

questions.hint: Prompt replies avoid losing a place and show reliability.

questions.prompt: Rashid changes his phone number after applying. What should he do?

options.text: Wait until he is invited to interview before mentioning it
Update his CV only, as that is what the panel reads
Tell the recruitment contact and update his account details
Do nothing, since only email is ever used

questions.hint: Contact details held by the department must be correct.

questions.prompt: The advert said results would be known by the end of the month, and it is now a week later with no news. What is reasonable?

options.text: A polite query to the named contact
Withdrawing her application
A post about the delay on social media
A message to a panel member she knows

questions.hint: A courteous query to the contact is proper once the stated date has passed.

questions.prompt: Which is a sensible use of the waiting period?

options.text: Reducing preparation so as not to be disappointed
Stopping all other applications until the result arrives
Contacting past colleagues for hints on what the panel will ask
Applying for other suitable roles and continuing to practise

questions.hint: Continuing to prepare keeps options open.

questions.prompt: A candidate posts the questions from her interview online to help others. What is the problem?

options.text: It is allowed so long as she does not name the department
It will lower her own score after the event
Questions are public documents once an interview has taken place
It can breach the process rules and disadvantage other candidates

questions.hint: Sharing assessment content undermines fair competition.

questions.prompt: A stage of the campaign is rescheduled by the department. How should Dina respond?

options.text: Read the message fully, update her calendar and confirm she can attend the new date
Assume the original date still stands until told again
Ask the department to keep the original date for her
Ignore it until a second message arrives

questions.hint: Changes need careful reading and a prompt response.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to ask a panel member directly about the result?

options.text: It will cause the application to be withdrawn automatically
Panel members are never allowed to speak to anyone
It bypasses the official process and could look like an attempt to gain an advantage
Panel members do not know the results

questions.hint: Queries go through the named contact so that all candidates are treated alike.

questions.prompt: Which note belongs in a simple tracker kept while waiting?

options.text: The names of other candidates and their likely scores
The reference, the dates of each stage, what was submitted and the stage reached
A copy of the department's internal planning papers
The home addresses of the panel members

questions.hint: A tracker records your own application and its dates.
